trial_name: CLIP-II — Cryopreserved vs Liquid-Stored Platelets for Surgical Bleeding (2025)
citation: Reade MC, Marks DC, Howe BD, Bailey MJ, Bannon PG, Eastwood GM, et al; CLIP-II Investigators. Cryopreserved vs liquid-stored platelets for the treatment of surgical bleeding: the CLIP-II randomized noninferiority clinical trial. JAMA. Published online December 8, 2025.
one_liner: In high-risk cardiac surgery patients requiring platelet transfusion, cryopreserved platelets did not meet noninferiority for 24-hour bleeding and were associated with increased bleeding and transfusion exposure.

pico.population: Adult high-risk cardiac surgery patients (ACSePT score ≥1 or clinician judgement) who required platelet transfusion intraoperatively or within 24 hours of ICU admission.
pico.intervention: DMSO cryopreserved group O apheresis platelets (up to 3 units) with open-label rescue platelets allowed.
pico.comparison: Standard liquid-stored platelets (buffy coat–derived pooled or apheresis, ABO-matched, up to 3 units) with rescue allowed.
pico.outcome: 24-hour ICU chest drain bleeding (noninferiority margin 20% increase).

background.existing_knowledge: Liquid-stored platelets require room-temperature storage and have short shelf-life (5–7 days), causing supply fragility, wastage, and 'platelet deserts'. DMSO cryopreservation at –80°C extends storage to years, but alters platelet phenotype (activation/procoagulant changes) and may affect haemostatic efficacy and thrombosis risk.
background.knowledge_gap: Modern, blinded comparative effectiveness data for cryopreserved platelets in major bleeding and cardiac surgery were lacking.
background.hypothesis: Cryopreserved platelets are noninferior to liquid-stored platelets for haemostatic effectiveness in high-risk cardiac surgery.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, noninferiority trial at 11 Australian tertiary hospitals (August 2021 to April 2024).
methods.setting: 11 Australian tertiary hospitals; postoperative ICU care.

inclusion: Adults at high risk of platelet transfusion (ACSePT score ≥1 or clinician judgement) undergoing cardiac surgery, not previously transfused platelets in current admission.
exclusion: Females aged 18–55 years with RhD-negative or unknown status; history of DVT or PE; coagulopathic conditions; other protocol-defined exclusions.

methods.intervention: DMSO cryopreserved group O apheresis platelets (up to 3 units), initiated intraoperatively or within 24h after ICU admission when platelet transfusion indicated.
methods.comparison: Standard liquid-stored platelets (buffy coat–derived pooled or apheresis, ABO-matched, up to 3 units).
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients and clinicians). Allocation concealed; blood bank and designated unblinded staff knew allocation.
methods.sample_size_power: 202 transfused patients (101/group) for 90% power with a one-sided 95% CI, noninferiority margin 20% increase (188 mL).
methods.primary_outcome: 24-hour ICU chest drain blood loss (geometric mean, ratio of geometric means).
methods.follow_up: 90 days for mortality and selected complications; hospital outcomes assessed.

headline_bullets: Noninferiority not met: bleeding ratio 1.13 (95% CI 0.96–1.34), upper CI 1.34 exceeds margin 1.20.
Cryopreserved platelets associated with higher total bleeding (1273 vs 972 mL) and greater transfusion exposure (RBC 52.9% vs 38.8%, FFP 75.0% vs 50.0%).
Rescue open-label platelet use substantially higher (42.3% vs 12.2%), suggesting reduced haemostatic adequacy.

outcomes_table.note: Noninferiority margin 1.20; upper CI 1.34 exceeds margin.
Cryopreserved group had significantly greater bleeding.

outcomes_table.outcome: Received RBC transfusion in first 24h in ICU
Received FFP transfusion at any time
Received cryoprecipitate transfusion at any time
Received open-label (nonstudy) liquid platelets at any time
Lowest platelet count in first 24h in ICU (×10^9/L)

outcomes_table.note: Trial not powered for mortality; interpret cautiously.

safety: Safety outcomes not formally compared; numerically higher mortality (12.5% vs 5.1%) and possibly other adverse events in cryopreserved group, but trial not powered for safety.

domains.notes: Central, computer-generated randomisation with permuted blocks, stratified by hospital; allocation concealed from treating clinicians and patients.
Double-blind design, but differential open-label platelet use (42.3% vs 12.2%) likely increased risk of unblinding and could influence subsequent transfusion decisions.

Primary analysis included only transfused participants (202/388), creating a modified ITT cohort vulnerable to selection bias. 92 and 94 participants per group were randomised but did not require transfusion and were excluded.

Incomplete protocol separation due to rescue; open-label platelet exposure significantly different, and early open-label use before completion of study platelets (25.0% vs 3.1%) further complicates analysis.
Baseline characteristics among transfused participants were broadly similar (age 66.9 vs 67.2 years; EuroSCORE II 4.5 vs 4.5; CPB time 137 vs 141 minutes).

Cryopreserved group received more study platelets (median 2 vs 1 units) and more total platelets; lowest platelet count in 24h significantly lower (103 vs 140 ×10^9/L), indicating reduced effective platelet replacement.
Greater exposure to FFP (75.0% vs 50.0%) and cryoprecipitate (71.2% vs 54.1%) in cryopreserved group, suggesting compensatory care and complicating attribution of bleeding outcomes.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity is moderate: randomisation and objective outcome measurement were strong, but the modified ITT analysis, substantial differential rescue platelet use, and likely partial unblinding reduce confidence that observed differences purely reflect platelet product efficacy.

domains.notes: High-risk adult cardiac surgery patients at Australian tertiary centres; findings most directly apply to similar cardiothoracic surgical populations.
Well-resourced tertiary centres; generalisability to low-resource hospitals, rural 'platelet deserts', and prehospital/military settings uncertain, despite these being key target use-cases.
Cryopreserved platelets were group O apheresis units reconstituted in plasma; performance may differ with other cryopreservation methods, storage durations, or ABO strategies.
This was cardiac surgery bleeding; extrapolation to trauma, obstetric haemorrhage, and medical thrombocytopenia cannot be assumed.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate for high-risk cardiac surgery in high-income settings using similar cryopreserved platelet manufacture and transfusion workflows, but limited for other haemorrhage contexts and the remote settings most motivated by platelet shelf-life constraints.

strengths: Double-blind, randomised multicentre design with stratification by hospital
Objective primary endpoint (24-hour ICU chest drain bleeding) with prespecified noninferiority margin
Pragmatic embedding into real-world perioperative bleeding management
Directly addresses a translational question: can a logistics-optimised platelet product replace standard platelets in major surgical bleeding?
limitations: Primary analysis included only transfused participants (202/388), weakening classic ITT protection against selection bias
Differential rescue/open-label platelet use (42.3% vs 12.2%) likely reduced blinding integrity and complicated causal attribution
Trial not powered to robustly assess uncommon safety outcomes or mortality; numerical imbalances cannot be definitively resolved
Cryopreserved platelets were group O and reconstituted in plasma; results may not generalise to other products, ABO strategies, or storage technologies

critical_appraisal.summary: CLIP-II was a well-designed noninferiority trial with objective endpoints, but the modified ITT analysis, differential rescue platelet use, and potential unblinding reduce confidence that the observed inferiority of cryopreserved platelets is solely attributable to product efficacy.
weaknesses: Modified ITT (transfused-only) weakens selection bias protection
Differential rescue platelet use likely compromised blinding
Limited generalisability beyond high-risk cardiac surgery

sections.authors_conclusion: In high-risk cardiac surgery patients requiring platelet transfusion, cryopreserved platelets did not meet noninferiority for haemostatic effectiveness and were associated with higher bleeding and increased transfusion exposure. Routine replacement of liquid-stored platelets with cryopreserved platelets is not supported.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Cryopreserved platelets should not replace standard liquid-stored platelets for routine use in cardiac surgery; they may serve as a contingency product during supply shortages.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: High-risk adult cardiac surgery patients in tertiary centers.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That cryopreserved platelets are completely ineffective; they may still be better than nothing when liquid platelets are unavailable.
implementation_caveats: If used as a contingency, anticipate higher bleeding and greater transfusion needs; ensure availability of rescue products and careful monitoring.

controversies.notes: The trial used a 20% noninferiority margin (188 mL) and a transfused-only primary analysis cohort (modified ITT), aligning with the pragmatic clinical question but reducing the protective features of a full ITT framework.

The large between-group difference in open-label platelet use (42.3% vs 12.2%) plausibly compromised blinding and may have contributed to downstream transfusion differences; accompanying editorial emphasised this as a key interpretive challenge.

A pilot RCT (CLIP-I) supported feasibility but was underpowered; an older bypass-era trial suggested potential differences in haemostatic performance, underscoring the need for contemporary, adequately powered trials (which CLIP-II provides).

Cryopreservation-associated platelet activation and functional change is well described; CLIP-II’s lower postoperative platelet counts and greater haemostatic product needs are consistent with reduced effective platelet replacement.
A subsequent economic evaluation based on CLIP-II data reported that cryopreserved platelets were not cost-effective relative to liquid-stored platelets under base-case assumptions.

Recent systematic reviews and transfusion guidelines provide evolving evidence, but direct evidence to support routine substitution of cryopreserved for liquid-stored platelets in major surgical bleeding remains limited.

context_related_trials.relation: Pilot RCT in perioperative bleeding that supported feasibility but was underpowered for definitive clinical outcomes.

unresolved_questions: Are cryopreserved platelets effective in other bleeding contexts (trauma, obstetrics)?
What is the optimal cryopreservation method, dosage, and ABO strategy to improve haemostasis?
Can improved products reduce bleeding and rescue transfusion needs?
What is the role of cryopreserved platelets in low-resource or remote settings where liquid platelets are unavailable?
What is the cost-effectiveness in contingency scenarios?

numbers_to_remember: Primary endpoint ratio 1.13 (95% CI 0.96–1.34) – noninferiority not met
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Cryopreserved platelets did not meet noninferiority for haemostasis in cardiac surgery and were associated with more bleeding and transfusion; they should not replace standard liquid platelets for routine use.
